nameStory: The name 'snail fur' perfectly captures what this tiny marine animal looks like when it colonizes hermit crab shells. From a distance, the fuzzy coating of countless tiny polyps makes the shell appear to have grown a soft, furry coat. It's as if someone gave a hermit crab's home a cozy sweater!
description: Snail fur is a colonial marine animal made up of hundreds of tiny polyps that grow together like a living carpet. These miniature creatures belong to the same group as jellyfish and sea anemones, but instead of floating freely, they form fuzzy, mat-like colonies on surfaces. The colony creates a soft, bristly coating that can completely cover a hermit crab's shell, giving it that distinctive 'furry' appearance. Individual polyps are tiny, but together they form colonies that can cover an entire shell.

idTips.label: Fuzzy shell coating
idTips.description: Look for hermit crab shells covered in what appears to be short, soft fur - the coating feels slightly bristly to the touch and moves gently in the current

idTips.label: Colonial structure
idTips.description: Close examination reveals the 'fur' is actually made of countless tiny, tube-like polyps packed tightly together

idTips.label: Shell association
idTips.description: Almost always found growing on empty gastropod shells occupied by hermit crabs, especially flat-clawed hermit crabs

idTips.label: Color variation
idTips.description: Colonies range from pale pink to orange-brown, sometimes with darker tips on the polyps

idTips.label: Texture response
idTips.description: When disturbed, the fuzzy coating may contract slightly, and individual polyps can withdraw into their tubes

habitat: Found in shallow coastal waters throughout New England, particularly in tide pools, rocky intertidal zones, and shallow subtidal areas. Look for them attached to hermit crab shells in areas with good water circulation, from the low tide zone down to about 30 feet deep.

seasonality.spring: Colonies begin active growth as water temperatures rise, with polyps extending fully and appearing most 'furry' during feeding.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for observation - colonies are most visible and active, with hermit crabs commonly found in tide pools and shallow waters.
seasonality.fall: Still active and easily observed, though growth may slow as temperatures begin to drop in later fall.
seasonality.winter: Colonies may appear less fuzzy as polyps contract more frequently in colder water, but still present on shells year-round.

funFact: Snail fur and hermit crabs have a mutually beneficial relationship - the hydroids get a mobile home and food scraps from the crab's messy eating, while the hermit crab gets camouflage and protection from the stinging cells in the hydroids' tentacles!
confusionNotes: Could be mistaken for algae or sponge growth on shells, but unlike these, snail fur has a distinctly fuzzy, hair-like appearance and will show tiny individual polyps under close inspection. Remember: if it looks like the shell grew fur, it's probably snail fur!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'snail fur,' this organism is actually more closely related to jellyfish than to any furry animal. The term 'hydroid' refers to the polyp stage of these cnidarians - they're essentially tiny sea anemones living together as roommates.
compareHints: Hydractinia echinata differs from its close relative H. symbiolongicarpus primarily in colony texture and polyp arrangement, though distinguishing them requires expert examination. Both species create furry coatings on hermit crab shells, but H. echinata tends to form denser, more uniformly fuzzy colonies. Other hydroids in New England waters typically don't form the same tight, fur-like mats on shells.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Hydractinia symbiolongicarpus is very similar to its relative Snail Fur (Hydractinia echinata), and the two are often difficult to distinguish in the field without microscopic examination.
